short: A quasilinear PCP theorem for PPAD

title.title: A quasilinear PCP theorem for PPAD
title.subtitle: Claim: End-of-Line reduces, with $N(\log N)^{O(1)}$ blow-up, to circuits that survive a fraction of bad gates

plain: Finding a balance point stays hard even if the answer may be wrong in a fixed fraction of places

beats.text: End-of-Line, schematically: from a known source, paths and cycles; find any other end
It is the canonical PPAD problem, behind Nash equilibria and fixed points
Claimed: robust numerical circuits encode it with only polylogarithmic blow-up

steps: Draw each path of the line puzzle as a curve in a box
Store each point with codes that survive many errors
Build a circuit that nudges points along the curves
Any near-solution, even with broken gates, is an end

achievement.label: PCP-for-PPAD conjecture (Babichenko–Papadimitriou–Rubinstein, 2016)
achievement.context: Before: constant-error hardness only with every gate satisfied (Rubinstein, 2016/2018)
achievement.note: Consequences for approximate Nash stay conditional

verify.detail: No Lean statement; at 147 pages, the longest TCS manuscript in the release
verify.ourCheck: We did not referee the proof; nothing here is machine-checked

voice.text: Finding equilibria is hard. Does it stay hard if some answers may be wrong?
Paths become coded curves that survive errors, so near answers still find an end.

sources.quote: The quasilinear PCP-for-PPAD conjecture was posed by Babichenko-Papadimitriou-Rubinstein (ITCS 2016)
constant-error hardness with every gate satisfied (Rubinstein 2016/2018)
a deterministic polynomial-time reduction from End-of-Line instances of length N to generalized circuits of total length N (log N)^{O(1)}
Under ETH for PPAD it implies stronger lower bounds for approximate Nash, but those consequences stay conditional.
Longest TCS manuscript in the release (147 pages), unformalized.
